title: Scientists use “empty space” to strengthen superconductivity
summary:
Scientists have shown that tiny changes called quantum fluctuations in empty space can strengthen superconductivity. The source report, published on October 3, 2026, calls this the first experiment to show the effect.

A superconductor is a material that carries electric current without electrical resistance under certain conditions. Its critical temperature is the temperature below which it becomes superconducting. Raising this temperature lets it work in slightly warmer conditions.

The study appeared in Nature. Changgan Zeng and Guanghui Cheng at the University of Science and Technology of China led it. Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and other partners also helped.

The team studied a surprising idea: empty space, called a vacuum, is not completely still. Even at its lowest energy, it has tiny quantum fluctuations. Scientists have seen effects of these fluctuations in other experiments.

Zeng explained that these fluctuations in ordinary empty space are usually too weak to have visible effects on large systems of materials. The team used a special structure called a terahertz dark cavity to strengthen their influence. It changes the electromagnetic surroundings of a material.

They put a superconducting material called NbSe2 inside the cavity. They compared how it worked inside and outside.

In a device with six layers of NbSe2, the critical temperature rose by up to 5.4%. Cheng reported that the critical current and critical magnetic field also rose greatly near the point where superconductivity begins. These are limits on the current and magnetic field the material can handle while staying superconducting.

The researchers changed parts of the experiment to test other explanations. Their checks ruled out effects such as strain, material damage and certain effects from nearby metal.

The improvement was greatest at one particular cavity frequency. Zeng said this was strong evidence that the superconducting state was interacting with electromagnetic patterns in the cavity. The findings offer a new way to study and control unusual states of matter.
why_it_matters: The experiment offers a new way to study and control superconductivity. A higher critical temperature allows the material to remain superconducting in slightly warmer conditions.
